---
title: Projection Integrals with Spherical Bessel Weights
---

This page is the technical description of how NumCosmo evaluates
$$
C_\ell^{XY} \;=\; \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \mathrm{d}k\, k^2\,
\left[\int \mathrm{d}\chi_1\, K^X(\chi_1,k)\, j_\ell(k\chi_1)\right]
\left[\int \mathrm{d}\chi_2\, K^Y(\chi_2,k)\, j_\ell(k\chi_2)\right],
\tag{1}
$$
a triple integral whose two inner factors oscillate. It is written as a problem
in scientific computing: the only property of the kernels used anywhere is that
each $K(\chi,k)$ is a smooth function of $\chi$ on a compact support, possibly
with a smooth $k$ dependence. A scale-dependent kernel is one where that $k$
dependence carries a factor such as $\sqrt{P(k,\chi)}$; nothing below depends on
what $P$ means, only on it being smooth.

The pipeline has two stages with a clean interface between them. The inner
stage computes, for one kernel and one $k$, the window
$$
I_\ell(k) \;=\; \int_a^b \mathrm{d}\chi\, K(\chi,k)\, j_\ell(k\chi)
\tag{2}
$$
for a whole block of consecutive multipoles at once
([The oscillatory integral](#the-oscillatory-integral) through
[Panels fixed in y](#panels-fixed-in-y)). The outer stage decides which $k$ to
ask for, builds a representation of $I_\ell(k)$ over $k$ for each kernel, and
integrates the product of two such representations exactly
([The window over k](#the-window-over-k) through
[The outer integral](#the-outer-integral)).

The inner stage is [[numcosmo-math|NcmSBesselIntegratorLevin]] over
[[numcosmo-math|NcmSBesselOdeSolver]], and the outer stage is
[[numcosmo|NcXcorKernel]] over [[numcosmo|NcXcor]]. Each section below names
the object it describes.

Every quantity that sets resolution is an output of a tolerance rather than an
input: the truncation order of each solve, the number of samples of each
kernel, the knot or panel count of each representation, and the range of $k$
integrated over. Two quantities are prescribed, and neither sets the accuracy
of the result: the panel grid in $y$ and the number of multipoles per block.

The figures on this page are produced by the library itself. The only objects
from cosmology are constructor arguments that the analytic test windows require;
the plotted quantities depend on them only through one smooth function $P(k)$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import spherical_jn, spherical_yn
from numcosmo_py import Nc, Ncm

Ncm.cfg_init()
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3})

cosmo = Nc.HICosmoDEXcdm.new()
dist = Nc.Distance.new(5.0)
dist.prepare(cosmo)
ps = Ncm.PowspecAnalytic.new(
    Ncm.PowspecAnalyticShape.BBKS, Ncm.PowspecAnalyticGrowth.LCDM
)
RH = cosmo.RH_Mpc()
```

## The oscillatory integral

The difficulty of Eq. (2) is entirely in $j_\ell(k\chi)$. Over a support
$[a,b]$ the weight completes about $k(b-a)/\pi$ oscillations, and a quadrature
rule needs several nodes per oscillation. The kernel $K$, by contrast, is
smooth and needs a few dozen samples however large $k$ is. Any method that
resolves the oscillations by sampling the integrand pays a cost in kernel
evaluations that grows linearly in $k$; the method below evaluates $K$ only
as often as its own smoothness requires and pays for the oscillations in a
banded linear solve.

### The dimensionless variable

With $y = k\chi$,
$$
I_\ell(k) = \int_{ka}^{kb} \mathrm{d}y\; F(y)\, j_\ell(y),
\qquad F(y) \equiv \frac{1}{k}\,K\!\left(\frac{y}{k}, k\right).
\tag{3}
$$
The weight no longer depends on $k$. Everything that is expensive to prepare
for $j_\ell$ can therefore be prepared once on a fixed grid in $y$ and reused
for every $k$, every kernel and every block of multipoles: only the integration
bounds $[ka, kb]$ and the forcing $F$ move with $k$. This is the organising
principle of the implementation ([Panels fixed in y](#panels-fixed-in-y)).

### From the integral to a boundary-value problem

The reduction below is what [[numcosmo-math|NcmSBesselIntegratorLevin]]
implements. $j_\ell$ solves the spherical Bessel equation; equivalently
$v(y) = y\,j_\ell(y)$ solves
$$
y^2 v'' + \left[y^2 - \ell(\ell+1)\right] v = 0 .
\tag{4}
$$
Let $u$ solve the same operator with a forcing,
$$
y^2 u'' + \left[y^2 - \ell(\ell+1)\right] u = y\,F(y).
\tag{5}
$$
Then the Wronskian-like combination $\mathcal{W} = v u' - v' u$ satisfies
$$
\mathcal{W}' = v u'' - v'' u = \frac{v\,yF}{y^2} = F\, j_\ell ,
$$
so on any interval
$$
\int_{y_a}^{y_b} \mathrm{d}y\; F(y)\, j_\ell(y)
 = \mathcal{W}(y_b) - \mathcal{W}(y_a),
\qquad
\mathcal{W}(y) = y\, j_\ell(y)\, u'(y) - \big(y\,j_\ell(y)\big)'\, u(y).
\tag{6}
$$
This is Levin's reduction [@Levin1996] specialised to the spherical Bessel
operator, and it is exact: no approximation enters until Eq. (5) is solved.
$j_\ell$ itself is evaluated only at the two ends of each panel. The unknown
$u$ is not free of oscillation: with Dirichlet data it carries homogeneous
solutions of Eq. (4), and its Chebyshev expansion needs about two coefficients
per oscillation of the panel, which is the floor $N_{\min}$ of [Incremental
Givens QR](sbessel_ode_solver.qmd#incremental-givens-qr). What the
reduction changes is where the oscillations are paid for. They cost $O(1)$
per coefficient in a banded linear solve and no evaluation of the kernel,
which enters only through the forcing $yF$ and is sampled as its own
smoothness requires.

Equation (5) is solved as a two-point boundary-value problem with homogeneous
Dirichlet data, $u(y_a) = u(y_b) = 0$, so that the second term of
$\mathcal{W}$ vanishes and the panel integral is $y_b j_\ell(y_b) u'(y_b) - y_a
j_\ell(y_a) u'(y_a)$. The unknown is $u = y\,w$ rather than $w$ (the solution
of the equation with the first-derivative term) because Eq. (5) has no
first-derivative term and no singular coefficient, which keeps the spectral
operator banded and well conditioned. The general form (6), with the $u$ term
kept, is what the code evaluates, because the extended cells of
[Panels fixed in y](#panels-fixed-in-y) solve on an interval larger than the
one integrated over.

```{python}
#| label: fig-levin-smooth
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Left: the integrand F(y) j_20(y) on the panel [100, 316] for a smooth forcing.
#|   Right: the solution u of the boundary-value problem (5) on the same panel, from
#|   the library's ultraspherical solver. It still oscillates, since the boundary
#|   conditions bring in homogeneous solutions, but the forcing needed 64 samples of
#|   the kernel and the solve is a banded linear system.
ell = 20
a, b = 100.0, 316.2278
m, h = 0.5 * (a + b), 0.5 * (b - a)


def F(y):  # a smooth bump in y, standing in for K(y/k, k)/k
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((y - 200.0) / 40.0) ** 2)


# Chebyshev coefficients of y F(y) on [a, b], then the C^(2) coefficients
N = 64
t = np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(N + 1) / N)
vals = (m + h * t) * F(m + h * t)
c = np.fft.rfft(np.concatenate([vals, vals[-2:0:-1]])).real / N
c[0] *= 0.5
c[-1] *= 0.5
c = np.concatenate([c, np.zeros(8)])
g = np.zeros(N + 1)
for kk in range(N + 1):
    g[kk] = c[kk] / (2 * (kk + 1)) - (kk + 2) * c[kk + 2] / ((kk + 1) * (kk + 3)) + c[kk + 4] / (2 * (kk + 3))
g[0] += 0.5 * c[0]

solver = Ncm.SBesselOdeSolver.new()
solver.set_tolerance(1.0e-12)
op = solver.create_operator(a, b, ell, ell)
coeffs, n_cols = op.solve(np.concatenate([[0.0, 0.0], g]))
coeffs = np.array(coeffs)

yy = np.linspace(a, b, 2000)
tt = (yy - m) / h
u = np.polynomial.chebyshev.chebval(tt, coeffs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
ax[0].plot(yy, F(yy) * spherical_jn(ell, yy), lw=0.8)
ax[0].set_xlabel("y")
ax[0].set_title("F(y) j_l(y)")
ax[1].plot(yy, u, lw=1.2)
ax[1].set_xlabel("y")
ax[1].set_title(f"u(y), {n_cols} Chebyshev coefficients")
plt.tight_layout()

# the boundary term (6) against composite Gauss-Legendre on the oscillatory integrand
du = np.polynomial.chebyshev.chebval([-1.0, 1.0], np.polynomial.chebyshev.chebder(coeffs)) / h
levin = b * spherical_jn(ell, b) * du[1] - a * spherical_jn(ell, a) * du[0]
gx, gw = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(20)
edges = np.linspace(a, b, 401)
ref = sum(0.5 * (e1 - e0) * np.sum(gw * F(0.5 * (e0 + e1) + 0.5 * (e1 - e0) * gx) * spherical_jn(ell, 0.5 * (e0 + e1) + 0.5 * (e1 - e0) * gx))
          for e0, e1 in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]))
print(f"boundary term {levin:.12e}   quadrature reference {ref:.12e}   rel. diff {abs(levin-ref)/abs(ref):.1e}")
```

### Derivative weights

Two further weights are needed, $j_\ell'(y)$ and $j_\ell''(y)$. They are
reduced to the plain weight by integration by parts, once and twice,
$$
\int F\, j_\ell' = \big[F\, j_\ell\big] - \int F'\, j_\ell,
\qquad
\int F\, j_\ell'' = \big[F\, j_\ell' - F'\, j_\ell\big] + \int F''\, j_\ell .
\tag{7}
$$
The remaining integrals are Eq. (3) with forcing $-y F'$ and $+y F''$. Both
are read off the same Chebyshev fit of $F$ that the plain case uses: the
derivative maps in the ultraspherical basis are banded (first derivative) or
diagonal (second derivative), so no extra evaluations of the kernel are needed.
The bracketed boundary terms use the fit's values and first derivative at the
panel ends and $j_\ell'$ from the recurrence $j_\ell' = j_{\ell-1} -
\tfrac{\ell+1}{y} j_\ell$, which is why a derivative-weighted block reads the
Bessel array one order below its lowest multipole.

## The spectral solver

Equation (5) is solved by [[numcosmo-math|NcmSBesselOdeSolver]], which
discretises it in the ultraspherical $C^{(2)}$ basis and grows an incremental
Givens QR until the solution coefficients decay. The discretisation, the
batching over multipoles, the truncation floor and the conjugate panel spans
are described on [The Ultraspherical Spectral
Solver](sbessel_ode_solver.qmd). Only two of its properties are used below: the
right-hand side is the $C^{(2)}$ expansion of $y F(y)$ with the endpoint values
in the first two entries, and the truncation order $N$ it returns is an output
of the tolerance, floored at about two coefficients per oscillation of the
panel.

## The forcing on a panel

The right-hand side of the discretised operator is the Chebyshev expansion of
$y\,F(y)$ on the
panel, computed adaptively: the function is sampled at Chebyshev--Lobatto nodes
$t_j = \cos(j\pi/2^k)$, whose grids nest so that going from level $k$ to $k+1$
evaluates only the new odd nodes, and the level is doubled until the
coefficients shared by two successive levels agree,
$$
\|c^{(2N)}_{0:N} - c^{(N)}\|_2^2 < \max\!\big(\tau_F^2\,\|c^{(2N)}\|_2^2,\; \epsilon_{\rm abs}^2\big).
\tag{8}
$$
The transform is a type-I DCT and the details are on the
[Spectral Methods](spectral.qmd) page. The default $\tau_F = 10^{-8}$ is the
looser of the two solver tolerances and therefore the one that bounds the
result; the ODE tolerance $\tau = 10^{-13}$ is well below it. Two consequences
follow. A kernel evaluated with noise above $\tau_F$ makes Eq. (8) fail on
every level, and the expansion refuses to return rather than returning a
wrong number. And anything fitted downstream to the samples this stage produces
cannot be asked for more than $\tau_F$;
[Two representations of the window](#two-representations-of-the-window)
enforces that.

The number of kernel evaluations per panel is set by the smoothness of $K$,
typically nine to thirty-three, and does not depend on how many oscillations
the panel holds. The oscillations are paid for in the solve, $O(N)$ per panel
with $N$ at least the floor $N_{\min}$, about two per oscillation. Kernel
evaluations dominate the cost of a call, which is what makes this split the
one to optimise.

## Panels fixed in y

The integrator keeps a fixed grid of knots in $y$, logarithmically spaced,
$$
y_i = 10^{-4 + i/2}, \qquad i = 0,\dots,20,
$$
two per decade from $10^{-4}$ to $10^6$. For each knot interval and each block
of multipoles the discretised operator is built and factorised once, and
$j_\ell$ at every knot is cached for every $\ell$ up to a cap. An integral over
$[ka, kb]$ is then the sum over the knot intervals inside it, each a replay of
stored rotations against a new right-hand side, plus two partial panels at the
ends.

The partial panels are where a moving bound meets a fixed cell. The forced
equation is solved on a fixed dyadic sub-cell of the knot interval that
contains the bound, the smallest one wider than the piece to integrate, so that
sub-cell operators are also reusable and never wider than twice what is
needed. The forcing is fitted on the true piece $[ka, y_i]$ only, so the kernel
is never evaluated outside its support, and the fit is rebased onto the
sub-cell by the exact affine change of variable. Since Eq. (6) holds for any
smooth extension of the forcing, $\mathcal{W}(y_i) - \mathcal{W}(ka)$ evaluated
from that solution is the integral over the true piece alone; this is why the
general boundary functional, with its $u$ term, is the one implemented. The
rebased polynomial can grow outside the fitting interval, so its norm is
checked against the fit's own scale and a cell that fails the check falls back
to an operator built on the exact piece.

Panels on which $y\,j_\ell(y)$ has underflowed at both ends for every
multipole in the block contribute exactly zero and are skipped before anything
is built or solved: this is what removes the region far below the turning point at
no cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ygrid
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The fixed knot grid in y (vertical lines) and the intervals [ka, kb] two different
#|   k values map a window on chi in [1000, 2000] onto. Interior knot panels are
#|   replayed from stored factorisations; the shaded ends are the partial panels.
knots = 10.0 ** (-4 + 0.5 * np.arange(21))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.2))
for yk in knots:
    ax.axvline(yk, color="0.6", lw=0.8)
for i, (k, col) in enumerate(((0.01, "C0"), (0.3, "C3"))):
    ya, yb = k * 1000.0, k * 2000.0
    inside = knots[(knots >= ya) & (knots <= yb)]
    ax.hlines(1 - 0.4 * i, ya, yb, color=col, lw=6, label=f"k = {k}: [{ya:g}, {yb:g}]")
    if len(inside):
        ax.axvspan(ya, inside[0], ymin=0.55 - 0.4 * i, ymax=0.75 - 0.4 * i, color=col, alpha=0.25)
        ax.axvspan(inside[-1], yb, ymin=0.55 - 0.4 * i, ymax=0.75 - 0.4 * i, color=col, alpha=0.25)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1e-4, 1e6)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("y = k chi")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
```

Three reuse axes fall out of this construction. Across $k$: the panels and
their factorisations do not depend on $k$. Across kernels: two kernels at the
same block and panel differ only in the right-hand side. Across multipoles: a
block shares one factorisation. The cost that remains per $(k,\text{kernel})$
is the Chebyshev fit of the forcing on each panel and one $O(N)$ replay per
panel, both set by the kernel's smoothness.

## The window over k

This stage is [[numcosmo|NcXcorKernel]], and its output is an
[[numcosmo|NcXcorKernelIntegrand]] holding one closure per kernel per block.

The inner stage returns $I_\ell(k)$, for a block of $\ell$, at whatever $k$ it
is asked. The outer stage has to decide the range of $k$ that matters, sample
it, represent $I_\ell(k)$ over that range, and integrate the product of two
such representations. In the library the block window is
$W_\ell(k) = p_\ell(k)\, I_\ell(k)$ with a smooth prefactor $p_\ell$ that the
kernel supplies, and the outer integral is Eq. (1) with $W$ in place of the
brackets.

### Domain expansion

The support in $k$ is found rather than prescribed, by
[[numcosmo-math|ncm_function_sample_set_expand_domain]]. A few seeds are placed
where each component of the kernel peaks, near $k \sim \nu/\chi$ for the
block's multipoles and the component's support in $\chi$. The domain is then
grown outward, alternately to the left and to the right by a factor
$1 \mp \alpha$ with $\alpha = 0.2$, and each new point is evaluated. Growth on
a side stops after five consecutive points with $\|W\|_2 < \epsilon\, W_{\rm
ref}$, with $\epsilon = 10^{-5}$ and $W_{\rm ref}$ the running maximum over
the block, or at a hard bound set by the range on which the kernel is defined.
Five consecutive small values distinguish a tail from a zero crossing of an
oscillatory window; the running reference protects against seeds that land on
a rising flank. The truncation error of the outer integral is then of order
$\epsilon$ for a window whose amplitude and integrand fall off together, and
larger for windows with power-law tails, where a pointwise criterion truncates
late.

### Several components

A kernel may be a sum of components with different supports in $\chi$, and
therefore different ranges in $k$. Each component is tracked separately during
the expansion and dropped from the sum once it is below $\epsilon\,W_{\rm ref}$
for five consecutive outward points, so that its radial integral is not paid
for where it cannot matter. Components whose supports in $\chi$ touch or
overlap are pieces of one window and are judged and dropped together, on the
norm of their sum: the $k$-space tail of a piece is set by its edges, the two
pieces cancel at the edge they share, and a piece cut on its own size would
leave its partner's uncancelled edge tail behind, an oscillation the true window
never had.

The sampled block therefore jumps where a component is dropped, by the
component's value there, at most $\epsilon\,W_{\rm ref}$. What is done about
that jump depends on the representation.

### Two representations of the window

Both representations are fits to the same samples on the same domain, and
either can be selected for a whole computation through
[[numcosmo|NcXcor]]:closure-type. The default is the Chebyshev one.

Cubic spline. The domain is refined by inserting midpoints where a held-out
test fails: a not-a-knot cubic spline is built from the accepted points only,
evaluated at the candidate, and the candidate is accepted when
$\|f - s\|_2 \le \tau_r \|f\|_2 + \tau_a\, W_{\max}$ in the norm over the
block, with $W_{\max}$ the smallest of the block's per-multipole peaks. The two
tolerances add, so the larger one decides where refinement stops. A jump is
handled by continuing a dropped component beyond its boundary as
$v\,\exp[-10^{10}\,\delta k/k_R]$: the sampled function stays continuous, one
cubic can span the boundary, and what remains is a jump in the first
derivative. At the default tolerances this costs nothing measurable. At a
large $\epsilon$ the refinement chases the $10^{-8}$-wide transition and the
cubic through knots with spacing ratios of $10^7$ overshoots between them;
this is a limitation of the spline representation at non-default settings.

Chebyshev panels. The domain is split into panels on which the whole block
is expanded on one Chebyshev--Lobatto grid, doubling the order from 9 to at most
33 nodes until Eq. (8) holds for every multipole, with $\epsilon_{\rm abs} =
\tau_a W_{\max}$; a panel that does not converge at 33 is bisected and its
evaluations discarded. Three rules constrain where a panel may sit and when it
may be accepted. First, every component boundary found by the expansion is a
panel edge, and while a panel is fitted each component is either on or off for
the whole panel, decided at the panel's midpoint, so the outer panel reads
exactly zero including at the shared edge. A jump fitted across a panel
instead produces an aliasing residual of order $(j/W_{\max})/\sqrt N$ in
Eq. (8), with $j$ the height of the jump: a $4\times10^{-5}$ jump on a peak of
$10$ passes a tolerance of $10^{-6}$ and fails $10^{-7}$, where the splitter
bisects to its width guard and gives up. As an edge the same jump costs
nothing.

Second, an accepted panel is checked against the expansion's own samples that
fall strictly inside it, which are independent of the Lobatto nodes and sit on
every component's scale; a panel whose first grid straddled a narrow peak
passes Eq. (8) on two levels of a small smooth function, and is caught here
and bisected instead. Third, the fit tolerance may not be tighter than the
sampler's $\tau_F$, which is enforced as a fatal check: below it the samples
are not a smooth function of $k$ and neither representation converges.

```{python}
#| label: fig-window
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The block window W_l(k) for l = 2..9 of a Gaussian window in chi (mean 1500, width
#|   300, cut at 4 sigma), as the Chebyshev closure represents it. Vertical lines are
#|   the panel edges; the expansion stopped where every multipole is below 1e-5 of its
#|   peak.
sbi = Ncm.SBesselIntegratorLevin.new(2, 9)
gauss = Nc.XcorKernelAnalyticGauss.new_full(dist, ps, 1500.0, 300.0, 4.0, sbi)
gauss.set_l_limber(-1)
gauss.prepare(cosmo)
cheb = gauss.get_eval_vectorized_full(cosmo, 2, 9, sbi, Nc.XcorKernelClosure.CHEBYSHEV)
lo, hi = cheb.get_range()
ks = np.geomspace(lo, hi, 3000)
W = np.array([cheb.eval_array(k) for k in ks])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
for i in range(0, 8, 2):
    ax.plot(ks / RH, W[:, i] / np.abs(W[:, i]).max(), lw=1, label=f"l = {2 + i}")
for i in range(cheb.get_n_panels()):
    _, pa, pb = cheb.peek_panel(i)
    ax.axvline(pb / RH, color="0.6", lw=0.7)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("k [1/Mpc]")
ax.set_ylabel("W_l(k) / max |W_l|")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
orders = [cheb.peek_panel(i)[0].ncols() for i in range(cheb.get_n_panels())]
print(f"{cheb.get_n_panels()} panels, coefficients per panel: {orders}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-closures
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The same window fitted by both representations: knots of the cubic spline against
#|   the panel edges of the Chebyshev expansion. The spline needs a knot every few
#|   oscillations; a panel holds up to 33 coefficients and covers as much as the
#|   oscillation count allows.
spline = gauss.get_eval_vectorized_full(cosmo, 2, 9, Ncm.SBesselIntegratorLevin.new(2, 9), Nc.XcorKernelClosure.SPLINE)
knots_k = np.array(spline.peek_knots().dup_array())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.0))
ax.plot(knots_k / RH, np.ones_like(knots_k), "|", ms=12, color="C0", label=f"spline knots ({knots_k.size})")
edges_k = np.array([cheb.peek_panel(0)[1]] + [cheb.peek_panel(i)[2] for i in range(cheb.get_n_panels())])
ax.plot(edges_k / RH, 0.4 * np.ones_like(edges_k), "|", ms=18, color="C3", label=f"Chebyshev panel edges ({edges_k.size})")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.4)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("k [1/Mpc]")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cut
#| fig-cap: >
#|   A two-component window (Gaussians at chi = 600 and 2600, widths 100 and 150) at l
#|   = 2..9. Each component is dropped where its own window falls below 1e-5 of the
#|   block, inside the domain of the other, so the domain has three segments: one
#|   component alive, both, one. Every interior panel edge (dashed) is a bisection of
#|   one of those segments rather than of the whole domain; the outermost two are the
#|   component boundaries themselves.
sbi2 = Ncm.SBesselIntegratorLevin.new(2, 9)
multi = Nc.XcorKernelAnalyticMulti.new_full(
    dist, ps, Ncm.Vector.new_array([600.0, 2600.0]), Ncm.Vector.new_array([100.0, 150.0]),
    Ncm.Vector.new_array([1.0, 1.0]), 4.0, sbi2)
multi.set_l_limber(-1)
multi.prepare(cosmo)
mc = multi.get_eval_vectorized_full(cosmo, 2, 9, sbi2, Nc.XcorKernelClosure.CHEBYSHEV)
lo, hi = mc.get_range()
ks = np.geomspace(lo, hi, 4000)
Wm = np.array([mc.eval_array(k)[0] for k in ks])
edges = np.array([mc.peek_panel(0)[1]] + [mc.peek_panel(i)[2] for i in range(mc.get_n_panels())])
frac = (edges[1:-1] - edges[0]) / (edges[-1] - edges[0])
dyadic = np.abs(frac * 2**16 - np.round(frac * 2**16)) < 1e-6
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
ax.plot(ks / RH, np.abs(Wm) / np.abs(Wm).max(), lw=1)
for e, d in zip(edges[1:-1], dyadic):
    ax.axvline(e / RH, color="0.6" if d else "C3", lw=0.8, ls="-" if d else "--")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(1e-8, 2)
ax.set_xlabel("k [1/Mpc]")
ax.set_ylabel("|W_2(k)| / max")
plt.tight_layout()
```

## The outer integral

Two closures of a pair, $W^X_\ell$ and $W^Y_\ell$, are each a single polynomial
between consecutive breakpoints: knots for a spline, panel edges for a
Chebyshev expansion. On every cell of the common refinement of the two
breakpoint sets, over the intersection of the two domains, the integrand
$k^2 W^X_\ell W^Y_\ell$ is therefore one polynomial, and it is integrated
exactly. No node, no adaptive step and no tolerance enter this stage; the only
error of the final $C_\ell$ is the closures' own fit error and the truncation
of the domain.

Two splines. The cell integrand is $k^2$ times two cubics, degree 8, and
five-point Gauss--Legendre is exact through degree 9. Both closures are
evaluated at the five nodes of each cell; the sum is the integral.

Two Chebyshev panels. On a cell $[k_a, k_b]$ with $k = m + h t$, each
closure's panel polynomial is restricted to the cell by the affine change of
variable, which is a change of basis and exact. Write the restrictions as
$W^X = \sum_i a_i T_i(t)$ and $W^Y = \sum_j b_j T_j(t)$. The weight is a
degree-two series in the cell's own variable,
$$
k^2 = \Big(m^2 + \tfrac{h^2}{2}\Big) T_0 + 2mh\, T_1 + \tfrac{h^2}{2}\, T_2 ,
$$
and it is folded into one side with the product rule $T_p T_j = \tfrac12
(T_{p+j} + T_{|p-j|})$, giving $\tilde b_j$ with two more terms. The cell
integral is then the bilinear form
$$
\int_{k_a}^{k_b} \mathrm{d}k\; k^2 W^X W^Y
 = h \sum_{i}\sum_{j} a_i\, \tilde b_j \int_{-1}^{1} T_i T_j\, \mathrm{d}t,
\qquad
\int_{-1}^{1} T_i T_j\, \mathrm{d}t = \frac{1}{1-(i+j)^2} + \frac{1}{1-(i-j)^2}
\tag{9}
$$
for $i+j$ even and zero otherwise, from $\int_{-1}^{1} T_n = 2/(1-n^2)$ for
even $n$. The form is $O(N^2)$ per cell with $N \le 33$; it is affordable
because the panels bound $N$.

A spline against a panel. A cell of the common refinement lies inside one
knot interval, so the spline is one cubic there, and interpolation at four
Chebyshev--Lobatto nodes reproduces a cubic exactly. The spline side is thus
turned into four Chebyshev coefficients and Eq. (9) applies. This is what
allows a pair whose two kernels sit in different regimes to be integrated
without either being refitted.

The error reported with $C_\ell$ propagates the closures' fit residuals,
$\delta(W^X W^Y) \simeq |W^X|\,\delta W^Y + |W^Y|\,\delta W^X$, integrated
with the same $k^2$ weight over the same cells. A spline records the residual
its refinement achieved on each knot interval; a Chebyshev panel records the
$\ell^1$ mass of the coefficients above the level its convergence test compared
against. Where no record exists the requested tolerance is used, which is a
ceiling rather than an estimate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cells
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The product integrand k^2 W^X_2 W^Y_2 for the Gaussian window against the
#|   two-component window, on the intersection of their domains. Vertical lines are the
#|   cells of the common refinement of the two panel sets; on each the integrand is a
#|   single polynomial and Eq. (9) integrates it in closed form.
xcor = Nc.Xcor.new(dist, ps, Nc.XcorMethod.KERNEL_EXACT)
xcor.set_ell_batch_size(8)
xcor.prepare(cosmo)
vp = Ncm.Vector.new(8)
xcor.compute(gauss, multi, cosmo, 2, 9, vp)

lo = max(cheb.get_range()[0], mc.get_range()[0])
hi = min(cheb.get_range()[1], mc.get_range()[1])
ks = np.geomspace(lo, hi, 6000)
prod = np.array([k * k * cheb.eval_array(k)[0] * mc.eval_array(k)[0] for k in ks])
e1 = np.array([cheb.peek_panel(i)[2] for i in range(cheb.get_n_panels())])
e2 = np.array([mc.peek_panel(i)[2] for i in range(mc.get_n_panels())])
cells = np.unique(np.concatenate([[lo], e1[(e1 > lo) & (e1 < hi)], e2[(e2 > lo) & (e2 < hi)], [hi]]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
ax.plot(ks / RH, prod / np.abs(prod).max(), lw=1)
for c_ in cells:
    ax.axvline(c_ / RH, color="0.6", lw=0.7)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("k [1/Mpc]")
ax.set_ylabel("k^2 W^X W^Y / max")
plt.tight_layout()

# exactness check: high-order Gauss-Legendre on the same cells, against the library
gx, gw = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(40)
ref = 0.0
for ca, cb in zip(cells[:-1], cells[1:]):
    kk = 0.5 * (ca + cb) + 0.5 * (cb - ca) * gx
    ref += 0.5 * (cb - ca) * np.sum(gw * kk**2 * np.array([cheb.eval_array(k)[0] * mc.eval_array(k)[0] for k in kk]))
ref *= 2.0 / (np.pi * RH**3)
print(f"C_2: library {vp.get(0):.15e}   GL(40) on the same cells {ref:.15e}   rel. diff {abs(vp.get(0) - ref) / abs(ref):.1e}")
```

## What is adaptive and what is prescribed

| quantity | how it is set | default |
|---|---|---|
| truncation order $N$ of each panel solve | adaptive QR, stopping test with floor (9) | $\tau = 10^{-13}$ |
| Chebyshev order of the forcing on a panel | level doubling until (11) | $\tau_F = 10^{-8}$ |
| panel grid in $y$ | prescribed, two knots per decade on $[10^{-4}, 10^6]$ | 21 knots |
| partial panels at the ends | smallest dyadic sub-cell containing the piece | --- |
| multipoles per block | prescribed by the caller | 8 |
| domain in $k$ | expansion until $\|W\| < \epsilon W_{\rm ref}$ five times | $\epsilon = 10^{-5}$, $\alpha = 0.2$ |
| component boundaries | same test per group of touching components | --- |
| spline knots | held-out midpoint refinement | $\tau_r = \tau_a = 10^{-4}$ |
| Chebyshev panels in $k$ | bisection with order cap, cuts at boundaries, sample check | cap $2^5+1$ |
| outer integral | exact on the common refinement | none |

Two floors remain that no tolerance moves. The sampler's own accuracy
$\tau_F$ bounds every fit made to its samples. And the result is a sum of
per-panel boundary terms that can cancel, so the attainable relative accuracy
is bounded by the cancellation ratio $\sum_p |I_p| / |\sum_p I_p|$ times the
machine precision; the per-panel record exists so that this ratio can be
measured rather than inferred.
